note: Drafted by the chat assistant 11-04 for the owner's review (D150 T03b, second wider-CS batch). Nothing is live until approved in Admin → Learn → Questions. 'pieces' are suggested Learn step ids to verify.

items.stem: A storage bucket holding customer exports was found readable by anyone on the internet. What's the right fix?
choices: Block public access at the account level, grant least-privilege access only to the roles that need it, and alert on any policy that makes data public
Rotate the access keys and change nothing else
Delete the bucket
Rename the bucket to something hard to guess
why: Account-wide blocking stops it happening anywhere, least privilege limits who can read, and alerts catch the next misconfiguration.
Public buckets don't need keys; rotating them changes nothing.
Loses the data the business needs, and the next bucket can repeat the mistake.
Obscure names get found; it's still public.

items.stem: Your cloud bill doubled in three months, and nobody is sure why. What do you do first?
choices: Move to a different cloud provider
Buy reserved capacity for everything straight away
Tag resources by team and service, find idle and oversized resources, right-size them, and commit to savings plans only for steady usage
Turn everything off at night
why: A huge project, and the same habits follow you.
Locks you into paying for the waste for years.
You can only fix what you can see; tagging shows where the money goes, and right-sizing plus targeted commitments cut it.
Breaks anything that needs to run at night.

items.stem: When one availability zone went down, your whole app went down with it. What do you change?
choices: Run on a bigger instance in the same zone
Rely on nightly backups
Spread instances across several zones behind a load balancer, and use a multi-zone database
Keep a copy in a second region that you'd switch to by hand
why: One zone is still one point of failure.
Backups restore data, not uptime, and take hours.
Traffic shifts to healthy zones automatically, so losing one zone doesn't take the app down.
Possibly useful for disasters, but manual switching means a long outage for a common failure.

items.stem: Engineers change infrastructure by hand in the console, and environments have drifted apart. How do you fix this?
choices: Write the manual steps up in a wiki
Manage infrastructure as code (for example Terraform), reviewed like any code, with the plan run in CI and drift detection on
Take a snapshot of every configuration each week
Allow only one administrator to make changes
why: The wiki goes stale and nothing enforces it.
Every change is reviewed, repeatable and visible, and drift detection catches anything changed by hand.
Shows the drift after the fact without preventing it.
Creates a bottleneck, and drift still happens.

items.stem: The business needs at most 15 minutes of lost data and back online within an hour if a region fails. What do you build?
choices: Restore from backups if it ever happens
Cross-region replication with automated failover, and a recovery runbook you test on a schedule
Nightly backups to another region
Multiple zones in one region
why: Untested restores routinely fail when you need them most.
Continuous replication meets the 15-minute target, automation meets the hour, and testing proves both actually work.
Up to 24 hours of data lost, and restores take longer than an hour.
Protects against a zone, not a whole region.

items.stem: Services inside your private network call each other using one shared, long-lived API key. What's the better approach?
choices: Trust the network, since it's private
Keep one master key in each service's environment
Rotate the shared key once a year
Give each workload its own identity with short-lived credentials (cloud IAM roles or service identities)
why: One compromised service can then reach everything.
The same single point of compromise, copied everywhere.
A leaked key works for up to a year.
Each service only gets what it needs, and credentials expire on their own, so a leak is small and short-lived.

items.stem: A penetration test finds SQL injection in your login form. What's the fix?
choices: Hide database error messages from users
Put a web application firewall in front of it
Use parameterised queries, check the rest of the codebase for the same pattern, and add a test
Escape quote characters in the input by hand
why: Hides the clue, not the hole.
A useful extra layer, but the code is still vulnerable.
Parameters keep data and code separate, so input can't change the query, and checking similar code fixes the whole class of bug.
Manual escaping misses cases and gets forgotten.

items.stem: An employee entered their password into a phishing page, and their account was taken over. What prevents this next time?
choices: More phishing training only
Require phishing-resistant sign-in (security keys or passkeys) and alert on unusual logins
Require longer passwords
Allow logins only from office IP addresses
why: Helps, but someone will eventually click.
Security keys and passkeys won't work on a fake site, so a stolen password alone isn't enough, and alerts catch what slips through.
A long password typed into a fake page is still stolen.
Breaks remote work, and attackers can work around it.

items.stem: A library you depend on has a newly published critical vulnerability. What do you do?
choices: Check whether you're actually exposed, upgrade or patch, and add dependency scanning in CI with a clear policy
Remove every dependency from the project
Fork the library and freeze it at the current version
Wait until there's an incident
why: Checking exposure sets the priority, patching closes it, and scanning catches the next one automatically.
Not practical, and you'd rewrite far more code than you'd secure.
You keep the vulnerable code and lose future fixes.
Critical vulnerabilities are often exploited within days.

items.stem: Your team is designing a feature that handles payment details. When and how should security be involved?
choices: A security sign-off just before release
A threat model early in design, with the team, walking the data flows and tracking each mitigation
A penetration test after launch
Copy a checklist from another project
why: Too late to change the design without delays.
Thinking through how it could be attacked at design time means the fixes are cheap and built in.
Finds problems when they're most expensive to fix.
A generic checklist misses this feature's specific risks.

items.stem: You discover that application logs have been recording users' passwords and other personal data. What do you do?
choices: Delete every log
Shorten how long logs are kept
Encrypt the logs
Stop logging those fields at the source, purge the affected logs, reset the exposed passwords, and restrict who can read logs
why: You lose the logs you need to run the service and investigate.
The data already logged is still exposed.
People with log access can still read them.
Redacting at the source stops new leaks, purging and resets deal with what's already exposed, and access controls limit the risk.

items.stem: You suspect an attacker is on one of your production servers. What's the right first response?
choices: Wipe and rebuild the server immediately
Isolate the server, preserve evidence, work out the scope, rotate exposed credentials, and follow your communication plan
Keep watching quietly before doing anything
Shut down every system in the company
why: You lose the evidence of what they did and how they got in.
Containing first limits the damage, evidence shows what happened, and scoping plus credential rotation stops it spreading.
The attacker keeps working while you watch.
Causes a huge outage for one suspected host.

items.stem: Your team checked an A/B test every day and stopped as soon as the result reached p = 0.04. What's the problem?
choices: Checking repeatedly and stopping on the first significant result inflates false positives; fix the sample size in advance or use a method built for peeking
There isn't one: p < 0.05 means it worked
Keep running it until p < 0.01
Split the users again and rerun it once
why: Deciding the stopping rule before you look, or using sequential testing, keeps the error rate honest.
Under daily peeking, the real false-positive rate is much higher than 5%.
Still peeking, just with a different stopping point.
Doesn't fix the peeking problem in either run.

items.stem: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together across a year. What do you conclude?
choices: With enough data, a correlation this strong shows causation
The data must be wrong
A third factor, summer, likely drives both; correlation alone doesn't show cause
Ice cream causes drownings
why: More data makes a confounded correlation more precise, not causal.
The data is fine; the interpretation is the issue.
Hot weather increases both, so you need to account for it before claiming either causes the other.
Correlation alone can't show that.

items.stem: Thirty percent of values in the income column are missing. What do you do?
choices: Fill them with the overall mean and move on
Find out why they're missing, impute carefully with a flag marking imputed values, and check whether it biases the results
Fill the missing values with zero
Drop every row with a missing income
why: Ignores why the data is missing and shrinks real variation.
Missingness often carries meaning, so understanding it and flagging imputed values keeps the analysis honest.
Zero is a real income and badly distorts the model.
You may throw away a biased third of your data.

items.stem: Marketing can only contact the top 1,000 customers most likely to churn each month. Which metric should guide your churn model?
choices: Precision among the top 1,000 (or lift at that cut-off), because that's the decision the model supports
ROC-AUC alone
Recall alone
Accuracy
why: It measures exactly what the budget allows: how many of the people you contact would actually have churned.
Useful overall, but it doesn't say how good the top 1,000 are.
Ignores that you can only contact 1,000 people.
Most customers don't churn, so accuracy looks high even for a useless model.

items.stem: Overall, the new checkout converts worse than the old one. But in every customer segment, it converts better. What's going on?
choices: Average the segment results together
The new checkout is worse
Ignore the segments and trust the overall number
The mix of customers in each version changed (Simpson's paradox); compare within segments or weight them consistently
why: A plain average can mislead in the same way.
The segment results say the opposite.
The overall number is the misleading one here.
A shift in which customers saw which version can flip the overall result, so a fair comparison holds the mix constant.

items.stem: A product manager asks, "Is this model good?" How do you answer?
choices: Compare it with a simple baseline and with the business outcome it changes, and say how certain you are
Say yes
Show detailed technical charts
Quote its accuracy
why: Good is relative: better than what we have now, by how much in business terms, and how sure we are is what they need to decide.
Overconfident, and it breaks trust if it underperforms.
Detail without meaning doesn't help them decide.
A single number without context doesn't answer the question.

items.stem: Two dashboards show different revenue for the same month. What's the lasting fix?
choices: Average the two
Use whichever number is larger
Ask each team which number they prefer
Define revenue once in a shared model or semantic layer, and build both dashboards from that one definition
why: An average is wrong in a new way.
Picking a number hides the problem.
Preferences don't fix two definitions.
One definition, used everywhere, means everyone sees the same number.

items.stem: After joining orders to customers, total revenue is suddenly three times too high. What's the likely cause and fix?
choices: Divide the total by three
Remove the join
Add DISTINCT to every column
The join is duplicating rows; check each side's grain and keys, and aggregate or deduplicate before joining
why: Only correct by coincidence, and wrong next month.
You lose the customer fields you needed.
Can hide the problem while still double-counting in subtle ways.
A key that isn't unique multiplies rows, so fixing the grain fixes the totals.

items.stem: Dashboards query billions of raw events directly and take minutes to load. What do you build?
choices: A larger warehouse
Restrict every dashboard to the last 7 days
Incremental modelled tables and aggregates (for example in dbt) that the dashboards read instead
Screenshots of the dashboards, refreshed daily
why: Costs more and still scans raw data.
Removes the history people actually need.
Pre-computed, incrementally updated models answer the common questions fast and cheaply.
Not interactive, and stale.

items.stem: A change to one dbt model silently broke three downstream reports. How do you catch this before it ships?
choices: Freeze all models
Check the reports by hand after each change
Add tests (unique, not null, relationships) and model contracts, and run only the changed models and their dependents in CI
Tell the team to be more careful
why: Stops all progress.
Slow and easy to skip.
Tests and contracts catch breaking changes, and running the affected models in CI shows the impact before merge.
Care isn't a control.

items.stem: Customers sometimes move region. Finance wants historical reports to keep showing the region a customer had at the time. How do you model it?
choices: Keep history with a type 2 slowly changing dimension (or snapshots): each version has valid-from and valid-to dates
Delete the old records
Overwrite the region when it changes
Make a separate table for each year
why: Each period joins to the version that was true then, so history stays correct.
Same loss of history, permanently.
History is lost; old reports change after the fact.
Hard to maintain, and it breaks queries that span years.

items.stem: Your incremental model misses events that arrive a day late. What's the fix?
choices: Rebuild the whole table every hour
Run the model more often
Ignore late events
Reprocess a lookback window (for example the last 3 days) on each run, merging on a unique key
why: Correct but slow and expensive.
More frequent runs still skip anything older than the last run.
Reports stay wrong.
Re-reading a short recent window picks up late data, and merging on a key avoids duplicates.
